# Architecture reference

Module structure, ownership boundaries and the shared settings/lifecycle/logging infrastructure. Read the section for the area you are changing.

## Build and packaging

Use `build.gradle.kts` and `app/build.gradle.kts` for current plugins, SDKs, Java level, dependencies, signing, and shrinking; `gradle/wrapper/gradle-wrapper.properties` for Gradle; `gradle.properties` for the project version. Release builds enable shrinking and may fall back to debug signing when the release keystore is absent. A release variant is not necessarily a stable-channel or production-signed artifact.

Direct release APKs compress DEX through the variant packaging API to reduce the distributed file size; this does not reduce uncompressed code or guarantee lower installed storage. Native libraries remain uncompressed and page-aligned for loading/injection. Release also limits resource locales, encodes final resource tables and uses Oz/ThinLTO for the native payload. The final encoding hook follows the pinned AGP task contract and must be revalidated on upgrades. Production R8 rules contain no test-only roots; isolated AICR contracts use `assembleContractProbe`, whose APK must not be installed/published or treated as exact-release evidence. See [size implementation and device evidence](../../docs/size/FINAL_SIZE_IMPLEMENTATION_20261028.md).

## Source map and ownership

Kotlin sources: `app/src/main/kotlin/com/takekazex/hypertweak/`.
- Directory ownership: UI pages are grouped under `ui/page/<feature>/`, shared dialogs under `ui/components/dialog/`; `Route.kt` remains in `ui/page/` for stable navigation identity. Utilities are grouped under `util/{logging,restart,scope,device,platform,diagnostics,update}/`. Hook support lives in `hook/preferences/`, `hook/runtime/{settings,reload}/`, `hook/nativebridge/`, and `hook/logging/`; `HookEntry`, `Preferences`, `NativeRules`, receiver and service entry names remain stable. SystemUI gesturebar/notification/controlcenter/lockscreen, icon carrier/left and SecurityCenter battery/sidebar/privacy each keep their feature family together.
- `hook/`: process entry and feature hooks; `hook/base/`: shared resolution and lifecycle infrastructure.
- `hook/bootstrap/`: explicit package/system-server installation plans and process-side settings participants. `HookEntry` retains DEX-session, loader, handle and generation ownership; participant coverage is validated before dispatcher registration. `ProcessLifecycleHooks` owns which concrete hookers run at process/context/hot-reload boundaries, so `HookEntry` imports no feature. Narrow a hooker to fewer processes only after checking where its targets run, such as the host manifest's `android:process` components, not from zero hit counts. Settings `:remote` hosts only services, receivers and `WifiProvider`, so page-only hookers are main-process steps there. Their participants return `true` in Settings side processes, because a `false` from an uninstalled hooker would retry the reload. Security Center follows the same rule: WarningCountdown, MoreBatteryInfo and the two AOSP entry hookers patch only main-process activities/fragments, while BerserkMode, DetailedPowerData and PowerRanking stay process-wide because remote services and providers read their static gates. `.github/scripts/check_architecture.py` also enforces hook internals: hook-root files and `base`/`runtime`/`preferences`/`nativebridge`/`logging` never reference `rules`; feature families reference only `rules.shared` plus the commented `FEATURE_COLLABORATIONS` allowlist.
- `settings/contract/`: storage-independent domain keys/defaults, shared lockscreen options, native Dock glass geometry, icon slot/control policies, signal artwork style and screenshot snapshot parsing. Callers use domain `*Keys` directly; `Preferences` remains the runtime read/write boundary without duplicate constant aliases. Storage diagnostics use `SettingsDiagnostics`, bound by `DebugLog` at process bootstrap, with a non-recursive platform fallback.
- `ui/`: Compose screens; `util/`: shared utilities, including `PlatformLevel.kt` for OS3/OS4 gates.
- `HookEntry` initializes processes; `Preferences` is the runtime/cross-process settings boundary; `BaseHooker` owns hook lifecycle. `hook/base/dex` owns feature descriptors, APK identity caches, serialized resolution and cancellable background preparation; `DexKitManager` is the native bridge backend; consumers use `DexRuntime` and `BaseHooker.prepareDexTargets` instead of managing bridge, worker, cache or cancellation state. APK identity revalidates by kernel stat (dev, inode, size, mtime/ctime ns): `ApkDigestStore` persists each installed APK's SHA-256 per host in `<host cache>/hypertweak_apk_digests.properties`, keyed by that stat and the build fingerprint, so process starts reuse it without reading the APK. A cache-only `DexRuntime.resolve` on the main thread never hashes: a cold identity returns a miss and the caller's background preparation hashes. Runtime settings refresh existing island policies without reinstalling or scanning DEX on the main thread.
- `ui/app/` owns the app Compose shell, observable setting values and persisted restart baselines. MainActivity injects the `AppSettingsStore` contract backed by `app/PreferencesAppSettings`; AppContent, AppSettingsState and AppRestartTracker share that store for effective migration reads, acknowledged writes, reset and flush. `MainActivity` retains Activity lifecycle/platform entry points. `AppContent` accepts a ComponentActivity, the Activity-owned UpdateManager and a module-status callback; it does not import MainActivity. `AppStartupEffects` owns launch effects; `app/AppActivationCoordinator` owns service-rebind/reinstall decisions and acknowledged first-run cleanup. Fresh-install evidence remains intact until cleanup succeeds. `ui/state/ReloadableSettings` uses the same readers for initial values and service-rebind/reset refreshes. The app shell also provides `LocalAppSettingsStore` to all navigation pages and dialogs; `AppSettingsStore` composes nine feature capabilities over the 12-operation `SettingsValues` storage port (backup, fingerprint, power button, back gesture, camera, launcher, SystemUI, platform and power saving); `ui/page` captures this port before invoking callbacks rather than importing Preferences. Effective migration readers, backup/restore, batched back-gesture writes and flush remain delegated to PreferencesAppSettings.
- `app/DefaultAppServices` wires the existing app-process managers through `ModuleServicePort`, `NativeUpgradePort` and `NativeRulePublisher`; `LocalAppServices` supplies the same lifetime instances to pages and deferred callbacks. UI sees immutable `ModuleServiceInfo` binding identities and process-name lists, without libxposed service/HookedTarget objects. Report/outcome/native-upgrade states, camera mode and notification icon policy live in `settings/contract`. Scope, restart, shortcuts, wireless diagnostics and update utilities receive storage/service/callback dependencies; none imports hook implementations. `app/AppServicePorts` is the app composition bundle, kept outside the storage-independent contract layer.
- Group IDs are declared once, in `RuntimeSettingsGroups`. `RuntimeSettingsDefinitions.groups` gives each ID its target processes and key sets: `keys` for owned keys, `strict` for owned keys whose snapshot value must be a Boolean, and `matches` only for ownership that is a policy rather than a list (`ICONS`). `strictBooleanKeys` is derived from the `strict` sets, so a key is written once; a strict key must be listed as strict in every group that owns it. `RuntimeSettingsGroups` builds a key→groups index on first use, and `owners` keeps declaration order. `RuntimeSettingsDefinitionsTest` checks that strict keys are Boolean catalog settings and that owner order holds.
- Settings transactions live in `SettingsMutationWriter`, injected with the existing backend, writer queue and locks. `RuntimeSettingsSnapshot`/`Ledger` are pure models; `RuntimeSettingsStore` owns the process ledger and invalidates `RuntimeSettingsReadCache` directly. `RuntimeSettingsProtocol` encodes the wire format, `RuntimeSettingsSignal` owns acknowledged publication, and authenticated sync receivers are separate from `SettingsTransport`. The vendored read-only preference facade receives a narrow reader from `Preferences`.
- `presentation/launcher/` owns the local desktop-icon illustration geometry. Its percentages are relative to the captured host baseline. SystemUI applies live sizes through the stock launcher provider; native structural hooks extend request/initializer bounds, while the frame observer caps sizes using active grid width and title padding.
- `presentation/icon/` and `presentation/glass/` own shared artwork, reduced signal models and rendering math used by both previews and hooks. They contain no hook registration. IME layout vocabulary, notification-header policy and volume-key policy live in `settings/contract/`; UI code must not import `hook.rules` for these shared contracts.
- `GestureBarEvents` feeds `GestureBarState`; `GestureBarHomeProbe`, `GestureBarDeadlines` and `GestureBarPresentation` own Home evidence, timers and reversible View effects. `HideBottomBarHooker` retains admission, recovery and retirement order. Home probes and deadlines use `GestureBarScheduler`, backed by the existing Handler and uptime clock, so pending work, deadline replacement and retirement are testable without Android handlers. `ControlCenterEditorAccess` owns plugin reflection and reversible listener/animation access. `NotificationHeaderCallbacks` resolves optional methods through `DexRuntime`; `NotificationHeaderClockSizing` owns native clock baselines and resource sizing, with hook handles retained by their parent hookers.
- `Preferences` remains the runtime access and acknowledged-write boundary. `SettingsBackupManager` orchestrates bulk replacement through its storage port; `AppLogStore` owns local log persistence/locking; `ExpiringReadCache` owns the short read memo. Bulk mutations and ordinary writes retain the single serialized writer and existing acknowledgement/rollback ordering. Synchronous writes that need the commit result go through `util/storage/commitEdit` (one editor, block, `commit()` returned); never chain raw `edit()...commit()` or use KTX `edit(commit = true)`, which returns Unit and drops a rejection.
- Portable settings backups export compact v2 JSON grouped by preference type, with decimal-string Long values and informational module/system metadata; v1 imports remain supported. Metadata never enters the restore map, and explicit defaults remain explicit. See [settings backup format](../../docs/SETTINGS_BACKUP_FORMAT.md) for compatibility and validation boundaries.
- Slider children consume the narrow `SliderSession` capability for class resolution and live flags. `SliderPercentageHooker` remains the composition/lifecycle owner; Common, Brightness and Volume do not depend on that concrete owner or each other.
- Callback settings use `hookSetting` volatile slots captured through `Preferences`; the existing snapshot acceptance/backend listener refreshes them before live effects. Declare an explicit cold-read default with `hookSetting(default) { ... }`; storage failures retain the previous/default value. Registry membership locks never cover storage reads. Keep storage reads inside captures or explicit setup migration readers. `ViewVisibilityRouter` owns SystemUI framework visibility/alpha hooks, while feature-owned subscriptions retire through `BaseHooker`. `ResourceValueRouter` owns the SystemUI `Resources.getColor(int,Theme)` / `getDimensionPixelSize` / `getIntArray` hooks: features subscribe entry names (plus optional packages) only while their switch is on, each reader is hooked on first subscription, and matches are cached per asset table in a `SparseArray`. Never add a second hook on these framework methods; framework-wide hooks that only serve one switch install on its first enable. See `docs/HOOK_IMPLEMENTATION_SECTION3_20261026.md`.
- `BaseHooker.generationState` owns transient field reset after host cleanup; `generationRequiredState` invalidates installation metadata, and `generationCleanup` provides idempotent resource/retirement fallbacks even when ordered restoration throws; `generationResource` clears caches under their own monitor; non-concurrent readers/writers must use that same monitor. `generationMainResource` synchronously retires UI-owned collections on main, acquiring their monitor only after dispatch so the caller never waits for main while holding it. `hostRecovery(HostRecoveryPhase, ...)` declares living-host recovery beside its feature. `saveHotReloadState` hands over only host objects that are still live (a view in a window, a manager the controller drives): the handed-over list is a strong reference, so a dead row carried once is carried by every later generation (left icons once reached 38 roots, and the first one, long detached, decided the home slots). Rows that merely detach, such as the home bar behind the lockscreen, are recaptured by their attach hooks. `StatusIconHotReloadRecovery` discovers SystemUI surfaces and dispatches dependency phases across the installed root/child tree.; do not add a central per-feature recovery list. Host and system inputs go through the `GenerationInputs` helpers on `BaseHooker`: `generationMainHandler`, `generationWorker`, `generationScope`, `generationRegistration`, `generationObserver` and `generationReceiver`. `prepareForHotReload` releases them before `onPrepareHotReload`: pending main messages are dropped, workers stop, scopes cancel and registrations unregister once. A deferred receiver registration that resolves after retirement never registers. Workers, scopes and handlers stay usable afterwards, because settings reloads and plugin sessions retire and reinstall the same hooker object; never wrap an executor in `generationResource` with `shutdown`, since the reinstalled object would keep the dead executor. Ordered listener/thread/View restoration that must run while an input is still attached remains in `onPrepareHotReload`. Receivers registered from the application-attach path go through `HostApplicationContext.whenPublished`: before `LoadedApk` publishes the Application, a registration is keyed on the bare `ContextImpl`, so the later unregister fails (`Receiver not registered`) and the retired generation's receiver survives hot reload. A deferred registration must re-check its own retirement. A receiver that `HookEntry` registers for every package, such as the restart receiver, is also retired by `HookEntry` itself, because hook plans list its hooker as a root only for some packages. See `docs/HOT_RELOAD_RECOVERY_20261026.md` for migration and evidence.
- **Generation memory retirement.** LSPosed loads every generation from memory, about 12 MB of `[anon:dalvik-DEX data]` per release build. A retired generation is freed only once nothing in the host process reaches its module loader. Any one of these pins it for the life of the process:
  - a module-class value stored in a host `ClassValue`; `HostMembers` and `ViewPropertyRoutes` use `RetiringClassValue`, retired last in `onHotReloading`. `GenerationRetirement` owns these process-wide steps and their order, plus the state handed to the replacement, including for processes the module skips; add a new process-wide step there, not in `HookEntry`;
  - a live module thread: bundled `Dispatchers.Default/IO` workers or a `DebugLog` worker recreated after retirement. The bundled kotlinx scheduler never retires its core workers, and terminating it is unsafe: a terminated scheduler throws on any later dispatch, on the host thread that resumes the coroutine (this crashed SystemUI when a main-posted `NativeRuleStatePublisher` detach closed a channel). Hook code therefore dispatches on `HookDispatchers.IO` (also the `generationScope` default): a plain pool whose threads all time out when idle, never shut down and with no Cleaner action, so retirement needs no teardown and a late dispatch just starts a short-lived thread. `check_architecture.py` rejects `Dispatchers.IO`/`Default` in hook code. `ModuleDispatchers.retire` remains a backstop: only if a `DefaultDispatcher-worker` of this generation's loader exists, it logs at INFO and shuts the scheduler down from main after a 15 s grace period;
  - a module `Class` key in a host cache, such as `ConnectivityManager.sMethodFlagsCache` or system_server's binder latency histograms keyed by a served module Binder class (`HostClassCaches.purge`);
  - a host-registered callback added late by the retiring generation: its hooks keep firing until the replacement swaps the handles, so a lazy `registerX` from a hook callback re-registers after `onPrepareHotReload` (this pinned every system_server generation through `AospImeSystemHooker`'s settings observer). `GenerationInputs` refuses registrations between retirement and reinstall; register lazily through the `generation*` helpers. A lazy path that keeps its own registration (a monitor object, a component owned by the hooker, a Java runtime) must check `BaseHooker.generationRetired` or its owner's retiring flag, set before the unregistering cleanup runs, and on the thread or monitor that cleanup uses;
  - an `Executors.new*` executor that is never shut down: the JDK wrapper registers a Cleaner action that references the executor's module `ThreadFactory`, and its default core threads never time out, so it pins the generation even with no work queued. `LockscreenChargingDetailHooker` created one in its object initializer, and while the feature was off the hooker never installed, so nothing shut it down; owners created lazily from hook callbacks (`XiaomiShadeBarEvents`, the back-gesture driver's `MiuiHapticFeedbackHelper`) can be recreated by a late callback after retirement. Hook code uses `HookExecutors.serial` (Java-callable) or `generationWorker`: no Cleaner action, daemon threads that exit when idle, so an executor that is never shut down pins nothing once drained. `check_architecture.py` rejects `Executors` factories in hook code;
  - a delivered Intent: `LoadedApk` sets the receiver's loader on the extras before `onReceive`, and in system_server that Intent is ActivityManagerService's own record, kept in its broadcast history. Receivers in host processes extend `ModuleBroadcastReceiver` (implement `receive`), which resets the loader afterwards; `generationReceiver` already does;
  - a module binder in a cross-process cycle, such as the app-bar handshake's `reply`/`lease`, released on finish.

  Even after the loader unloads, ART's `DexFile` finalizer can run before the ClassLinker unregisters the dex. ART then logs `Failed to close dex file in finalizer` and keeps the copy mapped. So the retiring generation hands its `DexFile` objects and a weak reference to its loader to its replacement (`RetiredDexFiles`), which closes them only after that loader has been collected. `DexFile.close()` clears the cookie that class definition reads even when ART cannot free the dex yet; closing while the retired generation can still load a class aborts the host in `DexFile.defineClassNative` (this soft-rebooted system_server once a retiring thread outlived the first close attempt). A new long-lived thread, executor, host callback or `Class`-keyed host registration must be retired in the same way. To check a long-lived host, run `.github/scripts/hot_reload_check.py rounds <apk>`: it installs as hot reloads and reports live module loaders (SIGQUIT trace), in-memory DEX and HyperTweak threads per scoped process; a leak grows by one generation per round. `hot_reload_check.py heap <process>` dumps a heap and prints the strong paths to module loaders; the dump pauses the host for seconds, and a touch on SystemUI meanwhile ANRs and restarts it. Third-party modules can also pin our loaders; add such an edge to `FOREIGN_EDGES` to skip it in the path report. The boot generation can stay pinned by an `IntentReceiverLeaked` stack trace that a host captured while a module hook was on the stack; it is one generation and does not grow. SystemUI does the same through `ViewRootImpl.mLocation`, the `WindowLeaked` stack captured when a window is added: an AOD window created while an `AODHooker` hook was on the stack keeps that generation until the window is removed. A module `View` left in a host view tree also pins its generation until the host drops it (an old build was seen held by SystemUI's island animation `fakeBigIslandView`); retirement must detach or restore the views it inserted. A torch callback that `FlashlightPageExitHooker` ties to a flashlight-page view lives until that view detaches, independent of hot reload.
- **Deoptimization.** `deoptimize(m)` only forces `m`'s own original body into the interpreter for the life of the process; it does not undo inlining of `m` into its callers. Deoptimize the compiled *caller* that inlines a hooked method, never a hot hook target itself, unless oatdump shows the target's own AOT code inlines another hooked method (`oatdump --oat-file=<odex/oat> --class-filter=C --method-filter=M --no-disassemble --dump:code_info_stack_maps`, then map `InlineInfo` rows to methods). `BaseHooker` logs one DEBUG `self-deoptimized hook target` line per hooker for review. Removing a deoptimization only takes effect in a new host process: hot reload keeps the already-deoptimized backup.
  - New hooks add no `deoptimize()` by default. Add one only after oatdump shows that a caller's AOT code inlines the hooked method, and then deoptimize that caller. A DEX call graph (DexSQL, DexKit) only lists candidate callers; it cannot show inlining, which exists only in odex/oat stack maps. oatdump does not cover JIT inlining.
  - About 250 older self-deoptimizations remain on cold paths. They are kept on purpose: removing them gains almost nothing, and a wrong removal silently disables a hook. Re-check one with oatdump and remove it only when simpleperf shows that method on a hot path.
- `hook/base/HookComponent` lends feature components their parent's loader, context and managed hook operations; components do not create lifecycle or handle stores. `HostMembers` caches reflective members/misses by actual Class identity, while `HostAccess` owns main-thread dispatch and framework traversal. Host reflection defaults to `HostAccess` (or the `cachedDeclared*` / `cachedPublic*` fluent extensions): keep declared/public/inherited lookup and explicit accessibility distinct, and include the full parameter signature. Exact/fluent APIs require an explicit `accessible` policy; never mutate a borrowed cached handle’s access flag. Existing structural selectors use `HostAccess.cached(type, contract, resultType)` with a unique key and immutable member metadata only; never cache live host values there. Do not add per-instance member tags, class-name-keyed dictionaries or hooker-wide loaded flags for varying runtime types. See `docs/REFLECTION_CACHE_20261026.md`. Cache hits select lazy lookup/accessibility tables by name and compare immutable full signatures by actual parameter Class identity. Only cold additions copy signature arrays and serialize publication; wrapper forwarding uses array bridges and no-argument overloads, while callers may still allocate their own vararg arrays. Java adapters use `HostAccess.requirePublicMethodArray` and the strict `requireInheritedField` entry (only NoSuchField is cached, access failures retry). The back-gesture name/arity compatibility resolver keeps its legacy semantics in a ClassValue/name/arity cache (including misses), without compound hit keys; it is not a general resolver API. Shell MOVE admission uses one persistent drain per session on the serial Shell owner, preserving the first threshold crossing and latest sample before terminal seal. Device microbenchmarks and cold/hot tradeoffs: `docs/HYPERTWEAK_PERFORMANCE_ARCHITECTURE_RESEARCH_20261113.md` §§12–14.
- **Hook DSL.** `hook/base/HookDsl.kt` owns `HookFactory`/`HookParam` and the `XposedInterface.Hooker` that `BaseHooker.hook {}` installs through `module.hook(target)`; EzHookTool is no longer a dependency (the Credits entry stays, because the DSL is ported from 1.3.1). `HostContext` owns the application context (`Application.attach` argument, else `ActivityThread.currentApplication()`; one attach hook per generation, retired as an old handle on hot reload). `HostReflect` keeps the library's other reflection results: `callMethodOrNull` picks the single most specific instance overload on the class chain, and class loading retries the last `.` as `$`. It keeps the EzHookTool 1.3.1 chain contract (`HookDslTest`): befores in order until one sets a result/throwable, then replace/intercept around the original, afters in reverse order even when skipped; a failing callback is logged and the call falls back to the unmodified original (`before`/`replace`/non-proceeding `intercept`) or to the outcome the failing `after` was given. One `HookParam` per call is shared by all stages, and arguments are copied from the chain only when a callback reads `args`. Hot-reload replacement builds the same hooker and calls `replaceHook`, with no reflection into library internals.
- **Host member selection.** Pick a declared host member through `hook/base/HostSelect` (`method`/`field`/`constructor` with `name`, `params` (null = any type at that position), `paramCount`, `returns`, `type`/`typeIs`, `static`/`instance`, `where(label) {}`). It returns a member only when exactly one matches, and otherwise returns null and logs `HostSelect ambiguous … candidates=…`. Bridge/synthetic methods match only after `synthetic()`, while constructors and fields are not filtered, because Kotlin default constructors and `this$0`/`val$` fields are real targets. Pass a feature-prefixed `key` to cache the result, including misses, per actual Class through `HostMembers`. `check_architecture.py` keeps `declared{Methods,Fields,Constructors}.firstOrNull/first` in hook code to a per-file allowlist that may only shrink. The remaining entries are hierarchy-walking helpers or contracts not yet verified on a host build. Before converting one, confirm uniqueness on the device APK (DexSQL `methods`/`fields`, excluding access flags `0x1040` for methods). The EzHookTool-style class-chain `findMethodOrNull {}` is gone: every hook target is a declared member chosen by `HostSelect`. A target the owner inherits is found by walking the levels explicitly up to a named base and selecting at the level that declares it (`LeftRenderer.managerCallback`: `MiuiLightDarkIconManager` inherits `onSetIcon`/`onRemoveIcon` from `IconManager`), so a later host override is picked up and a class outside that hierarchy yields nothing.
- **Failure boundaries.** Hook callback bodies do not wrap themselves in `runCatching`. The dispatcher catches a failing callback, falls back as described above, and counts it per hook id. Optional steps inside a callback, and per-frame or installation steps outside one, use `HookFailurePolicy.open(scope, operation, fallback)`. Persistence and app-process calls add `.onFailure { DebugLog.w(...) }`. Both the dispatcher and `HookFailurePolicy` log through `FailureLogBudget`: the first 3 failures of one site carry their stack, after that only the 10th, 100th, 1000th and so on are logged as one-line summaries. A failure that repeats on every frame therefore stays visible without flooding the log. A dropped `runCatching` result is legitimate only on cleanup, hot-reload and restore paths, and `check_architecture.py` caps the total in hook code; the cap may only fall.
- **Hook hit counters.** Every dispatch increments an unsynchronized per-(hooker, hook id) counter in `HookHits`. `su -c am broadcast -a com.takekazex.hypertweak.action.DUMP_HOOK_HITS [--ez reset true]` makes each process with the restart receiver log, at INFO under tag `HookHits`, its window length, per-hooker totals with zero-hit counts, and the 25 hottest ids; `reset` starts a new window; hooks whose callbacks failed are listed as `failing … failures=N` (never reset). system_server has no such receiver: `RestartBroadcastHooker` refuses the `android` context that system_server's packages publish, because a receiver there runs on system_server's looper (an escaped dump exception crashed it and RescueParty rebooted the device on 2026-11-26). `onReceive` catches everything at that boundary. Use the dump as evidence for narrowing process scope or choosing hot paths, never as proof of visible behavior.
- `SystemUiSettingsHost` owns icon/AOD/header/notification live-setting effects. `HookEntry` retains process generations, DEX sessions, loaders and managed handles.
- Status-bar icons are layered: settings → shared host hooks → state hubs → pure plan → mask applier and renderers → handover. Details per layer:
  - **Settings**: `IconConfigDecoder` is the single decoder. Retired keys are read only through `IconConfigMigration` (an explicitly stored current key wins, even at its default; otherwise the retired key applies) and are never written; they migrate through `IconConfigMigration.LAST_MIGRATING_VERSION` (1.9.4) only, and `IconConfigMigrationTest` fails once the version passes it so the object is deleted. Typed stores that cannot return raw values look up the stored type with `IconConfigMigration.legacyType`. Slot modes come from `SlotsIconConfig.slotModes`, never from a raw store read. `Preferences.iconConfig()` serves runtime hooks; UI, preview and debug use the same decoder. `IconConfigReload.domains` diffs two `IconConfig`s per section to choose live refresh, scoped reload or the full transaction. Signal-style changes refresh policy, cellular gates and the mobile/stacked pipeline, reload only native type configuration, and reconcile Duo only when entering/leaving Duo; they do not retire Wi-Fi, battery or shared host adapters. The same diff applies to changed full snapshots with no key list; unchanged full snapshots recover living hosts without rebuilding groups. SVG style changes use the existing renderer asset refresh instead of a full transaction. The stacked bitmap key includes the loaded SVG source hash as well as levels and render config, so an artwork-only change republishes at unchanged signal strength; a pending asset load retains the last verified holder.
  - **Shared host hooks**: renderers (`IconRenderer` / `IconRenderComponent`) never hook icon host methods directly; they `observe` through `IconHostHooks`, which installs one hook per executable and fans callbacks out by `hostCallbackOrder` via `HostCallbackRegistry`. A renderer reload closes only its subscriptions, so host hook order cannot change. `IconHostHooks`, `PanelMotionAdapter` and `MobilePipelineAdapter` come first in `SystemUiSettingsHost.iconHookers()`. Panel targets resolve through `prepareDexTargets` on the worker and register on main; before publication the host remains native. Publication schedules scoped living-host recovery, reading the delegate callbacks and current expansion flows even if the ordinary recovery barrier already ran; BaseHooker retirement cancels pending publication.
  - **State hubs** (`MobileSignalHub`, `NetworkHub`, `PanelHub`): each has one producer (`MobilePipelineAdapter`, `WifiPipelineAdapter`/`WifiPipelineSource`, `PanelMotionAdapter`), outlives consumer generations and replays the current value on subscribe (`ReplayState`). Consumers read the hub; they never keep a pushed copy. Publishing goes through `IconMainThread`, which runs inline on main and posts otherwise; it never blocks a host thread. Hot reload rebinds the Wi-Fi source at `HostRecoveryPhase.SOURCES`; `StatusIconHotReloadRecovery` fills `HostScope.coroutineScope`/`wifiInteractor` before that phase. Until it binds, `NetworkHub` has no transport or Wi-Fi level, so Duo stays native and the carrier rows report `missing=[wifi]`. `PanelHub.prepare(next)` hands `beforeMotion` subscribers the state the pending host step will publish; no feature hooks the control-center panel callbacks itself (the privacy chip consumes `PanelHub` too). `MobileSignalState.settle` keeps the shown mobile state through a host rebind of the same SIMs.
  - **Plan**: `presentation/icon/IconLayoutPlan` is pure. Renderers submit `Claim`s (owner, surface, parts, ready, priority); user hiding wins, then ready claims by priority, and a whole-`MobileRow` claim also covers its bars and type label. The preview and `SlotClaimRegistry` (container-local claims, resolution cached per config and actual surface; Duo supplies its binding surface and AOD phase) call the same function.
  - **Duo expanded signal**: `icon_duo_expanded_signal_style` (0 native, 1 stacked; default 0) chooses expanded cellular bars independently of `icon_duo_expanded`'s battery style. `IconConfig.hasStackedSignal` enables artwork publication and the native standalone type pipeline; `stackedSignalOn` and the plan admit the Duo stacked destination only on `CONTROL_CENTER_EXPANDED`. Other containers ignore its shared holder, and it never starts a standalone stacked motion from HOME. Duo's existing stacked endpoint handover handles arrival. Carrier claims retain priority, and status-bar-only SIM filtering releases the expanded stacked destination to native rows. Changing the option refreshes policy, cellular gates, native type, mobile/stacked and Duo owners; it does not rebuild icon groups. Artwork selection is shared with ordinary stacked mode. Missing/invalid settings preserve native expansion, and existing holder cleanup/recovery handles hot reload and upgrades.
  `DuoSignalArtwork` retains both one-row and two-row contour families for the accepted weight. Wi-Fi's single dot row and the dual-SIM ring request them alternately during the same pre-draw; a last-key-only cache repeatedly parses SVGs and samples PathMeasure on main. Weight changes and generation retirement invalidate both families; ordinary frame updates reuse their contour identities.

Each frame is derived from those alone (`IslandPullDownFrame`): the children of `getFakeExpandedView()` scale from the top to the outline, capped at 1.6, and blur through the host's static `setMiSelfBlurCompat`, at 40 × progress while background material is open. Before `DynamicIslandWindowViewController.add/updateDynamicIslandView`, the flashlight entry (sbn package `miui.systemui.plugin`, channel `flashlight_channel`, focus `param_v2.business == "miui_flashlight"`) gets `FlashlightIslandPanel` as `view` and a second, non-interactive panel as `fakeView`; the big and small islands keep their template. The panel is the plugin's own flashlight page: `layout/mi_flashlight_layout` inflated with the plugin class loader (body container, `mi_seekbar_bg` track, `MiVerticalSeekBar`), its `mi_fl_view` stub replaced by `layout/mi_flashlight_static_effect` with the `mi_flash_low_close` / `mi_flash_long_light` / `mi_flash_compose_light` bitmaps, which is the effect `MiFlashlightUiFolme` installs (the OpenGL `FlashlightRender` is not reused). The read-back is synchronous on SystemUI's main thread at the start of a host transition, so it is half size, into one reused bitmap, and a second request within 150ms (a hide followed by its re-add) reuses the first. It calls `exitMiniWindow` for the parked flashlight island and answers with the island's screen bounds (content view X + `getBigIslandX()`, `getBigIslandViewWidth()`, `getIslandViewHeight()`). The flight starts at an estimate (cutout − 36dp … cutout + 9dp, the icon-only big island; height from `island_height`) and eases onto the answer, 35% of the gap per frame. `ExitMiniWindow` natively collapses with `MiniWindowToBigIsland`, a morph from the expanded geometry (for this island the 200×320dp panel, which read as a box). While our restore dispatches (500ms window, one-shot), a before-hook on `ResolveFromMiniWindowKt.resolveFromMiniWindow` replaces that for a `BigIsland` target that is not temp-hidden with the native `HiddenToBigIsland`, so the pill grows from the cutout while the page shrinks into it. The page opens through the window view directly, never through `DynamicIslandSafeguardsController.enterMiniWindow`, so the controller is captured from `delayDeleted(key, seconds)` on flashlight island updates and from `exitApp`. Within 3s of such an early restore, the native `exitApp` for the plugin is skipped, because its close-end state would run again on an island that is already back. Without the signal, the after-hook still restores the island once the page closes. Group `plugin.flashlight_page` delivers the switch to that process. `miui.systemui.plugin` is also loaded inside SystemUI, so force-stopping it kills SystemUI: `RestartScopeSelection.SHARED_WITH_SYSTEM_UI` keeps it out of the restart picker, `RestartUtils` and `RestartRootScript`.
- Control Center island hide (`ControlCenterSuperIslandHooker`). The host's combined `tempHidden` can stay false when only Control Center changes, so the hooker forces `isTempHiddenExt` and dispatches `onIslandTempHide` itself. Like the native `registerTempHiddenChanged` collector, it first calls `DynamicIslandWindowState.setTempHiddenChange(TRUE)`. `preHandleEvent` keeps that mark only for `IslandTempHiddenChanged`. Restores read it through `TransitionContext.isTempHiddenChange` and resolve `TempHiddenTo*`, whose `temp_hidden_to_show` → `showIslandLayout` → holder `onShow` resumes module animations (native Lottie, HyperSpectrum). Without the mark, a restore resolves as `BigIslandChanged`, and holders stay paused after `show_to_temp_hidden`.
- Camera profile access is shared through `CameraConfigAccess`; `CameraMasterLiveHooks` owns the donor/effect/focal/probe feature family. `MediaEditorWatermarkResolver` discovers/validates `WatermarkContract` targets before its parent installs them. `ImeRaiseController` owns keyboard padding/caption injection state and upgrade restoration.
- JVM tests: `app/src/test/`. Scope metadata: `app/src/main/resources/META-INF/xposed/scope.list`; also inspect `app/src/main/res/values/arrays.xml` when changing scope presentation or checking release parity.

## Settings storage and transport

Host preference caches are optional storage capabilities. `Preferences.initLocalCache` publishes a usable context/cache pair only after checking the context's data directory and opening its preferences; a system/provider context without application storage continues to use the remote configuration and does not abort package-ready dispatch.

## System server readiness

`SystemServerReadinessHooker` observes the framework boot-phase boundary. Assistant/gesture settings recovery probes live content/role services, binds observers before alignment, uses bounded polling windows and rearms pending work on lifecycle events. `SettingBackupTransaction` requires acknowledged backup/live writes and retains originals after failed restoration. `NativeRules` binds JNI only for the exact launcher owner; status inspection never loads a library, and a failed load is not repeatedly retried in an unrelated process.

## Logging

`DebugLog.isEnabled(priority)` gates expensive diagnostic reflection/task submission before it runs;
the inline Kotlin `d(scope) { message }` also avoids a capturing closure when disabled. Java
back-gesture diagnostics require both module DEBUG and the existing VERBOSE tag opt-in.
Keep outcome/audit messages on the eager hook-skip/WARN/ERROR helpers: their explanation
counts precede filtering. Do not gate functional collectors or state updates with log levels.

`util/logging/DebugLog.kt` owns severity, bounded dispatch and counted repeat suppression. `bootstrap/ProcessLogging` injects a live level reader through `LogBackend`; only the module Application receives the existing AppLogStore sink. Cold/hot hook entry binds a level reader without a persistence capability. Retirement flushes before dropping the binding; the logger never imports Preferences. `LogRecord`/`LogCodec` is the shared wire format; errors retain stack traces and expected preference/process skips use DEBUG. Detailed hook registration, target resolution and high-frequency rendering diagnostics belong at DEBUG; INFO describes meaningful runtime state changes. Do not classify severity from words inside a message, and do not silently swallow failures at shared resolver, persistence or system-callback boundaries.

App records are stored by the existing AppLogStore; LogRepository receives its read-only snapshot capability from ProcessLogging and never imports Preferences; injected processes forward to the LSPosed logger, without attempting to write hook-side remote preferences. App log buffers/session/process selections and obsolete per-process log thresholds are local-only at every typed getter/setter, including synchronous strings. Only module Application initialization grants access to this store; injected host caches are never log destinations. On application service binding, the serialized writer removes historical app-log keys from the daemon without clearing shared recording/log-level controls, setting revisions or local app records. A rejected cleanup retains its deletion keys independently of the mutable remote shadow, reports failure, and retries on the next binding. Reset/restore and rollback cannot reintroduce those keys remotely. `LogRepository` merges app records with `LsposedLogReader` records selected by exact module identity. The log page refreshes on entry/service rebinding or an explicit tap, displays source/process/PID, and exports the same snapshot. Reading LSPosed files requires root permission granted to HyperTweak; denial, missing files, timeout and read failure remain visible while app logs are still available. Reads are limited to the four newest active module log files, 2 MiB per file and 2,000 module entries. It does not modify framework files or collect other modules into the snapshot. A single global log level applies to the app and every injected process. Session rotation/clearing only clears app records. The diagnostic provider uses the same repository and retains its own/root/shell caller restriction.

## Runtime performance ownership

- `StackedRenderer` owns a bounded `RetiringWorker`: retirement closes the executor and fences old IO/publication, re-arm creates a fresh owner, and idle workers time out after 30 seconds. Historic workers created by older APKs require a process restart. Preferences, root-command and log-reader executors also release idle threads after 30 seconds, retaining their existing queue/receipt rules.
- `IconSvgRepository` reuses validated documents by current source SHA-256 and kind; hash changes reparse, concurrent cold loads serialize. Document bitmap caches obey both 48 entries and 4 MiB; eviction never recycles host-borrowed bitmaps. `PanelGlyphFrame` compares reusable primitive/reference snapshots, reuses its sampling Canvas and tint filter, and reuses ink analysis only after pixels compare equal. Dirty dynamic views still draw/sample.
- Notification seconds ticks require enabled, attached, shown, window-visible and interactive clocks. A weak pre-draw demand watch restores visible clocks; screen/time/configuration broadcasts and a 12/24-hour content observer restore/invalidate cached format state. Retirement removes observers, demand watches and pending ticks. Temporary long-press modes keep their existing expiry owner.
- `DebugLog` exposes lifecycle-owned control listeners for accepted settings and Android log-tag changes. App-bar functional flows remain bound; its three diagnostic flows exist only while both the module threshold and tag permit them. Retirement removes control callbacks and disposes optional/functional resources independently. Audit/problem counts retain eager semantics.
- The battery power-save monitor creates its receiver/provider observer/worker only when either feature is enabled. Accepted settings create the first owner without restart; disabling both closes it. A later enable reads the latest sticky battery state with a fresh reconciler.

## Notification-shade media switching

The OS4 media-card style uses the media-card live-settings group. An unset `media_card_carousel_style` reads the previous `media_card_swipe` switch, preserving existing AOSP selections. Style 0 uses the system single card, 1 uses AOSP, and 2 uses the HyperOS pager. The HyperOS pager reads MIUI's own sorted media candidates and creates one native `miui_media_session` view, MIUI binder, seek model and disposable coroutine scope per session. Each page includes the native media header and material binder, so shade glass, blur and normal backgrounds follow the host's material state. Pager layout synchronizes each nested header's `ExpandableView.actualHeight` so Android hit testing reaches its playback controls and card actions. The native Miuix page indicator follows the scroll position and is shown for multiple pages. Media touch uses the notification row's pressed scale. Long press binds a separate native media header and player in a full-screen status-bar sub-panel matching the native notification modal. It maps the pressed card through screen coordinates, moves the copy and action group together, and centers both using the native modal item spacing, collapsed notification height and bottom reserve. The original card is revealed again when the copy returns. A dedicated ModalWindowManager from the host factory drives the same blend blur, glass and solid fallback for this window without changing the stock row modal. The stock row modal itself requires a NotificationEntry. Close pauses the selected session and hides its card until playback resumes or the session ends. Hide app filters the current user's matching app only in this carousel. Restore hidden apps is available in the modal or directly in the media section when the filter leaves no pages. The filter is in memory and clears when leaving the HyperOS style or restarting SystemUI. Pages retain their order and selected identity across media updates and consume horizontal input through their own platform scroller. Each binder detaches and releases playback progress when its page disappears. AOSP remains a separate renderer. The notification header hosts SystemUI's Compose `Media` carousel, using the host factory and its media repository. When the legacy manager is active, its already-filtered user entries feed the Compose repository. The bridge releases only entries it published. The MIUI player stays available until the Compose view measures a nonzero area. The notification dismissal recognizer yields to the pager for touches that start in it, and stack scrolling uses the native vertical handler. Only the unlocked notification shade mounts this view. Disable and hot reload dispose the composition and restore the MIUI player. The control-center MiPlay card uses a separate plugin controller.

## Independent media Super Islands

The default-off `media_super_island_multi_session` preference is applied by the SystemUI island settings participant. SystemUI's current-user, active and dismissal-filtered media list supplies the candidates. The feature takes over when at least two cards are playing and keeps surviving cards registered until they stop. A session-owned task key namespaces the card notification key, while the host media instance ID deduplicates stale notification aliases. Each island has its own normal and animation holders, media binder, seek model, progress owner, and cancellable coroutine scope.

The native controller still consumes its top-media callbacks. During takeover its single-task add and remove are held, and the module invokes its native template builder with plugin lookup suspended on the main thread. The temporary controller fields are restored after each build. The plugin receives independently keyed adds and updates through the native content interface and arbitrates the normal island slots. The plugin's single pending media view reuse is skipped for these keys, so a newly added card cannot take over another card's animation view. A retired task is deleted without animation and releases its callbacks and seek observer. Disable and hot reload retire the feature-owned cards and resume the native publisher. The next generation recovers from the living Dagger component and the native media list, including an upgrade from a build without saved feature state.

## Runtime settings reload and hot reload

`RuntimeSettingsGroups` registers setting ownership, destinations and resync authorization.
Every explicit live-settings group uses the common snapshot/dispatcher: icons, islands,
screenshot, back gesture, native launcher settings (including the Dock glass), volume-key steps, XMSF focus
authentication, gesture-bar surfaces, security/offline checks, Security Center privacy and
warnings, cross-package clipboard and bubble notifications, and the SystemUI domains added
by the 2026-10-22 live-settings audit (`systemui.aod`, `.keyguard`, `.notification_header`,
`.notification_text`, `.media_card`, `.control_center_plugin`, `.glass`, `.lockscreen`,
`.power_save`). The 2026-11-01 completion adds `system.power_button`,
`system.experimental_capabilities`, `camera.configuration`, `systemui.monet` and
`settings.module_entry`. Power entry hooks remain installed for first enable; native AON
controllers refresh on their own handlers, and PWM capability caches restore the vendor flag.
Cached Settings/camera screens rebuild with native saved state on their next resume; the
structurally resolved recording-state reader prevents camera recreation during recording.
Camera registry additions and watermark cache entries have explicit retirement ownership.
Notification-header, resize, bottom-text and camera settings no longer mark ordinary edits
as pending restarts. See `docs/LIVE_SETTINGS_COMPLETION_20261101.md` for contracts and boundaries.
Participants re-derive policies on living hosts; optional hooks use the
managed on-demand installation lifecycle. The keyguard battery row uses `AodKeyguardPolicy`: an
explicit host phase from `MiuiFullAodManager.isDozing` (`mToLockScreen` alone is not a dozing flag) keeps the native row in every
lit/unknown state, and only the accepted ordinary Duo switch replaces it; AOD options apply
only in AOD phases, and every suppression sets one release-able ownership flag.
Snapshots carry their committed changed keys, so a domain that owns several hooks
routes each key to the hooker that applies it. Status-bar icon keys are routed by
`IconConfigReload.domains` (a per-section `IconConfig` diff): slot visibility/left placement/CC row split, Duo,
stacked and the network pipeline reconcile living views in place, and control-center,
lock-screen, native-type and single-slot owners are recreated alone through
`StatusIconHotReloadRecovery.scheduleScoped`. Neither path rebuilds the native icon groups.
Pipeline getters stay hooked while their option is off and return the host flow combined with a
`LiveFlowGate` (host `FlowKt.flowCombine`) or a module flow that re-publishes, so the bound
binder re-emits. Only structural keys (Duo/stacked switches, signal style, separate type, slot
order, pipeline slot modes, system-hide/privacy) keep the full transaction. A switchable feature never substitutes
zero for "no override" (corner radius) and keeps the host request separate from the
module suppression (lockscreen status bar).
`Preferences` commits complete acknowledged subsets through
`RuntimeSettingsSignal`; `RuntimeSettingsReceiver` delivers per-destination scoped snapshots
to `SettingsReloadDispatcher`. On attach a host requests its snapshot once and retries
(250/1000 ms) only until the module answers; each request can cold-start the module process,
which HyperOS records as an auto-start. Boot/package receivers that only recover a feature
(`SystemHelperStateReceiver`, `WirelessAdbStateReceiver`) stay manifest-enabled but are
switched off through `WakeReceiverGate` while their feature is unused. Legacy saved scopes cannot invent defaults for newly migrated
features. Bulk reset/restore uses the same acknowledgement and rollback path.

`ManagedHookReload` / `BaseHooker.replaceChildren` own hook recreation and host state recovery;
islands use fresh instances. The vendored back runtime reads the common preferences facade.
Native launcher delivery remains an output/host adapter, with their old
independent settings inputs removed. API-102 replacement cancels dispatch, carries the
scoped primitive snapshot, closes old observers and resumes registered participants after
restoration. Dedicated native binary updates retain their own acceptance boundary; Java hook
replacement is governed by the lifecycle and recovery contracts above. See `docs/RUNTIME_SETTINGS_RELOAD.md` for architecture
and `docs/HOT_RELOAD_TEST_CHECKLIST.md` for the complete test inventory.
